# Rule: canonical-ownership

Keep each explicitly modeled assertion in its canonical owner. Before creating a resource, inspect the closest owner and references; edit that resource when responsibility is already represented there. Use a separate resource only when it has a distinct responsibility or lifecycle. State whether a resource expresses intended structure, a normative rule, or an observed fact. Do not treat a generated projection, adapter observation or passing check as a replacement for the canonical assertion. Organize new typed resources by responsibility first and kind second, choosing the narrowest useful owner within the configured Project Areas.

Declare every modeled relationship through the loaded Domain's typed fields and relation descriptors. Each relation's context, invalidation and cycle behavior is explicit. Prose links help people navigate but do not create dependencies. Keep customer policy and provider-specific instructions in their owning domain and configure the appropriate adapter mapping rather than encoding them in Core.

For new Projects, recommend `.markitect/areas/<responsibility>/` as the canonical resource root, with nested folders for narrower ownership as needed. This is a convention, not a required layout. Existing Projects continue to use their explicitly configured Area paths; do not propose or perform a migration just to adopt this convention. A filename such as `change-review.workflow.yaml` may make kind discoverable to readers, but it is optional: the YAML `kind` field remains authoritative and filenames never infer type.

For ordinary documentation, start at an explicitly configured documentation root and follow local README routers toward the narrowest plausible owner. Compare configured Area paths, router scopes and nearby canonical documents. A path is an ownership clue, not proof of semantic placement. Find and update an existing owner before creating a second document. README links provide human navigation only; they do not create dependencies. Keep local completeness as a review heuristic, not a compiler claim.
